newsitem.title: CANADA: High yield grain a stopgap to Asia water shortfall.
newsitem.headline: High yield grain a stopgap to Asia water shortfall.

text.p: Higher yielding varieties of grain may serve as a partial and temporary stopgap solution to declining aquifers in some of Asia's major producing regions, a grain scientist said.

"With declining water availability in the North China Plain and in the Indo-Gangetic Plain will research be able to bridge that (production) gap? I think within limits research will help us to bridge that gap but in the end it's buying us time to think of a better integrated solution," International Maize and Wheat Improvement Centre director general Timothy Reeves told the Canadian Farm Writers' conference here.
Wheat crop output in northern China and India's Punjab state should drop as aquifers in both regions fall, Worldwatch Institute president Lester Brown told the conference on Thursday.
Brown's book "Who Will Feed China?" predicted China may import 200 million tonnes of grain a year by 2030 on growing population and declining grain production.
World cereal grain production will have to increase 2.5 percent a year to feed the same proportion of people the same amount of food as is currently consumed, Reeves said.
"We get it through pushing up yields, more efficient transformation of water, nutrients and sunlight," he said.
Wheat yields by selective plant breeding alone have increased one percent a year since the late 1960s, he said.
"If today's food output were at 1970 yields, we'd need 250 million hectares (620 million acres) more land," Reeves said.
Meanwhile, the amount of grainland per person dropped to 0.12 ha (0.30 acres) in 1994 from 0.18 ha (0.45 acres) in 1970, he said.
The Mexico-based agency, known as Centro Internacional de Mejoramiento de Maiz y Trigo, does research in 120 nations.
